verdicts.trueWording: unreliable, intensely subjective and seemingly incapable of analysing his experiences
verdicts.note: Chapter 10 Summary, live Cambridge Core page: the sentence naming Severian as 'just such a narrator' carries the quoted phrase word for word, in Wright's own voice, immediately after the Borges passage.

verdicts.trueWording: a narrator who omitted or corrupted what happened
verdicts.note: Same Summary paragraph: the words are Bioy Cesares's scheme in the Borges passage Wright quotes, and Wright applies it to Wolfe explicitly ('an analogue of the Borgesian character'), then to Severian. Page attributes the words to Borges's character rather than to Borges speaking directly.

verdicts.trueWording: expedites the reader's trust in the veracity of the document
verdicts.note: Chapter 7 Summary, third sentence: 'Wolfe's employment of a first-person narrator' precedes the quoted phrase, so both the first-person limb and the trust-in-veracity limb are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: told him then (as I had been taught)
verdicts.note: Chapter 7 Summary quotes the Agilus scaffold passage; the eleven quoted words appear exactly, and the training limb is carried by the parenthesis and by 'Severian, in his role as headsman'. But the word 'guild' occurs nowhere on this page (checked case-insensitively over the whole fetched document), so the institutional attribution is the claim's own addition.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the executioner's GUILD - the page grounds the training only in '(as I had been taught)' and 'his role as headsman', never in a guild

verdicts.trueWording: the introduction of ambiguity and ellipsis
verdicts.note: Chapter 3 Summary: the phrase is item two in the list introduced as 'four artful strategies', and the controlling limb is the preceding clause about compelling the reader to endure Wolfe's perception of life.

Chapter 3 Summary, final sentence: Wolfe 'aids this avoidance by disclosing the unreliability of his narrators in one of two ways', the first being the quoted phrase. The page confines it to the 'less intricate narratives' and pairs it with a second, commoner method; the claim asserts no exclusivity, so no limb fails.

verdicts.trueWording: a disjunction between what is apparent from a narrative's plot
verdicts.note: Chapter 5 Summary: after quoting Sanders on audience and performance, Wright's clause 'invariably indicates' the quoted disjunction, completed on the page by 'and what is occurring at the level of its story'.

verdicts.trueWording: he 'pretends not to see' his operator
verdicts.note: Chapter 5 Summary carries the quoted clause exactly, but the mechanism on the page is pretence, not blindness: the Joruri gloss it rests on says the operators 'stand in full view of the audience, but the audience pretends not to see them', and the narrator likewise 'pretends not to see' his operator. Flattening that to 'not seeing' inverts the point of the figure.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: by NOT SEEING his operator - the page says he pretends not to see an operator standing in full view

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe's stories and novels reflect one another
verdicts.note: Chapter 11 Summary: 'John Clute has already acknowledged how' precedes the quoted words, and the block closes with the citation '(Strokes, p. 160)', matching the claim's attribution and page.

verdicts.trueWording: pattern of responses to ... the prison of the self
verdicts.note: Chapter 11 Summary: Wright reports that Clute 'believes that the repetitions found in Wolfe's oeuvre represent' the quoted pattern, cited to '(Strokes, p. 161)'. Wright dissents in the next clause, but the claim only reports Clute's reading, which is what the page attributes.

verdicts.trueWording: ruins, bones, obscure relics with forgotten purposes
verdicts.note: Chapter 4 Summary: 'Commercial mines sunk into these strata yield fragments of mysterious, lost ages' introduces the quoted list, so the mines limb and the forgotten-purposes limb are both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: its geology having long succumbed to layer after layer
verdicts.note: Chapter 4 Summary, second sentence: the planet is 'one vast relic', its geology 'having long succumbed to layer after layer of archaeological remains'. The claim's 'buried under' is a fair rendering of 'succumbed to'.

verdicts.trueWording: Severian's memoir, written 10 years after he becomes Autarch
verdicts.note: Chapter 4 Summary: 'The Book of the New Sun is' precedes the quoted words, and the sentence continues to the faultless recall that lets him record his youthful experiences. Numeral '10' is the page's own form.

verdicts.trueWording: science fiction story told with the outlook, the flavour of fantasy
verdicts.note: Chapter 6 Summary, opening clause: the page frames the quoted words as 'Wolfe's definition of science fantasy', so the own-words attribution holds; Wright immediately calls the definition ambiguous.

verdicts.trueWording: not the result of a series of mystical unions
verdicts.note: Chapter 6 Summary, final sentence: Severian's progression into the manifold is the quoted negation 'but a consequence of an entirely chemical assimilation', which supports both limbs of the claim.
